item.title: ISO 5230, 18974, and 42001 Comparison
item.description:
1. Relationship Among the Three Standards

A company that develops AI systems using open source stands at the point where three standards intersect.

flowchart LR
 subgraph oss["Open source management"]
 A["ISO/IEC 5230\nLicense compliance\n(licenses, SBOM, artifacts)"]
 B["ISO/IEC 18974\nSecurity assurance\n(vulnerability detection, response, CVD)"]
 end

 subgraph ai["AI system management"]
 C["ISO/IEC 42001\nAI management system\n(governance, risk, life cycle)"]
 end

 oss -- "Open source compliance\nwithin AI systems" --> ai

ISO 5230 and 18974 are standards for managing open source itself, while ISO 42001 is a standard for managing AI systems. The two areas are independent, but they intersect when AI systems use open source.

item.title: 1. Context of the Organization and Leadership
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §4 and §5 are the foundation of the AI management system. They determine which AI systems the organization operates, who the interested parties are, and on what principles top management will manage AI.

From the perspective of open source practitioners, §5.2 (AI policy) is the most important point of intersection. Including principles on open source use in the AI policy makes it possible to operate it in an integrated way with the ISO 5230 policy.

item.title: Open Source Management in AI Systems
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §8.5 (AI system life cycle) and §8.6 (AI data management) cover requirements that must be managed during the AI system development stage. From an open source perspective, the key is license compliance for the open source components used in AI systems.

2. §8.5 AI System Life Cycle: Managing Open Source Frameworks and Models

2.1 Planning and Design Stage

When selecting the open source frameworks and models to use in the planning stage of an AI system, review their licenses in advance.

item.title: 2. Planning
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §6 requires a systematic way to identify and address risks and opportunities related to AI systems. In particular, §6.1.2 (AI risk assessment) and §6.1.4 (AI system impact assessment) are used directly to include risks that can arise from open source components.

2. §6.1.2 AI Risk Assessment: Including Open Source Risks ★

ISO/IEC 42001 requires a process to identify, analyze, and evaluate risks related to AI systems. Open source practitioners must explicitly include open source license risks and security vulnerability risks in this process.

item.title: AI SBOM
item.description:
1. What is an AI SBOM?

An AI SBOM (AI System Bill of Materials) documents a list of every element that makes up an AI system, along with its source and license. It extends the concept of the software SBOM (ISO/IEC 5230 §3.3.1) to AI systems and is the key deliverable for the ISO/IEC 42001 §7.5 (Documented information) requirement.

Why an AI SBOM Is Needed: Transparency and Regulatory Compliance

The AI SBOM is a key means of securing transparency and explainability of AI systems. ISO/IEC 42001 Appendix C.2.11 states transparency and explainability as key objectives of the AI management system.

item.title: 3. Support
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §7 covers the competence, awareness, communication, and documentation needed to operate the AI management system. From the perspective of open source practitioners, §7.2 (Competence) and §7.5 (Documented information) are the key points of intersection.

2. §7.2 Competence: AI Open Source Management Competence ★

ISO/IEC 42001 requires that persons performing AI-related roles have the necessary competence. From an open source compliance perspective, AI development and operations staff should have the following competencies.

item.title: AI Supply Chain Verification
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §8.8 requires appropriate evaluation and verification when using AI systems (models, APIs, services) procured externally. From an open source perspective, the key is the procedure for verifying license, security, and supply chain risks when procuring external open source AI models.

2. Three Types of External AI Procurement

Type Examples Open source relevance
Direct use of open source AI models Downloading Llama, Mistral, or Falcon model weights High: the license applies directly
AI services based on open source Hugging Face Inference API, Ollama Medium: the license of the underlying model must be checked
Commercial AI APIs OpenAI API, Google Vertex AI Low: terms of service apply (OSS licenses do not apply directly)

Types 1 and 2 are areas where open source licenses apply directly and are the main subjects of §3 to §4. Type 3 (commercial AI APIs) is also required in the same way by ISO/IEC 42001 §8.8, so it is covered separately in §5.

item.title: ISO/IEC 42001 Guide
item.description:
This guide explains, from the perspective of open source practitioners, the key requirements of ISO/IEC 42001 (AI Management System) that intersect with open source management. It provides practical guidance on what must be complied with when using open source frameworks, pre-trained models, and training datasets in AI systems, and on how to structure an AI SBOM.

Author : OpenChain Korea Work Group / CC BY 4.0

What is ISO/IEC 42001?

ISO/IEC 42001:2023 is an international standard for an AI management system (AIMS, AI Management System) that enables organizations to develop, operate, and manage AI systems responsibly and transparently.

item.title: 4. Operation
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §8 covers the actual operation stage of the AI management system. From an open source perspective, §8 is the section with the most points of intersection.

Subclause Description Open source intersection
§8.1 Operational planning and control Operating the open source review process
§8.2 to 8.3 AI risk assessment and treatment (during operation) Responding to OSS vulnerability risks
§8.4 AI system impact assessment (during operation) System impact of OSS vulnerabilities
§8.5 AI system life cycle ★ OSS framework and model licenses
§8.6 Data for AI systems ★ Open dataset licenses
§8.7 Feedback interface -
§8.8 Procurement of external AI systems ★ Supply chain verification of external OSS models

2. Detailed Pages

item.title: AI SBOM Compliance Guide
item.description:
This guide explains, one by one, each requirement of AI System Bill of Materials: Compliance Management Guide for the Supply Chain (Version 1.0), published by the OpenChain AI Work Group. It describes what verification materials each clause requires, how to comply, and what samples and tools can be used directly.

This specification carries the structure of the open source license compliance standard ISO/IEC 5230 (requirements, verification materials, rationale) over to the AI supply chain. It brings into the scope of compliance not only code but also the license and transparency obligations of model weights, training datasets, and the Model Tree.

item.title: 5. Performance Evaluation and Improvement
item.description:
1. Overview

ISO/IEC 42001 §9 and §10 cover the cycle of confirming whether the AI management system is achieving its intended results and improving where it falls short. From an open source perspective, §9.1 (Monitoring and measurement) is linked with open source compliance metrics.

2. §9.1 Monitoring and Measurement: Open Source Compliance Metrics ★

ISO/IEC 42001 requires monitoring and measuring the performance of the AI management system. Integrate existing open source compliance metrics into the performance indicators of the AI management system.

item.title: 7. AI Compliance
item.description:
Requirements Covered in This Section

ISO/IEC 42001: §5.2 (AI Policy) · §6.1.2 (AI Risk Assessment) · §7.5 (Documentation) · §8.5 (AI Lifecycle) · §8.6 (AI Data) · §8.8 (External AI Procurement)

AI systems make extensive use of open source frameworks, pre-trained models, and open datasets. Companies that operate an open source management system (ISO/IEC 5230 · 18974) must apply open source compliance principles during the AI system development phase as well. In addition, development environments that leverage AI coding tools (GitHub Copilot, Claude Code, Cursor, etc.) require a new management framework to address license contamination and the introduction of vulnerable packages.
